<meta>This page is the author's preface to the reader. It follows the title page which introduced Herman Moded as the author of this 1603 work against Anabaptist sects. In this preface, Moded explains the origins of the book and his collaboration with a former Anabaptist, Pieter Pauwels.</meta>

### To the Christian Reader.

Attentive Reader / as I still find here and there among the well-practiced **Brothers of the Cross** <term>Cruys broeders: A term for fellow Protestants who suffered persecution or exile for their faith.</term> / whom I especially love / so I also found a few years ago at **West-Souburg** <note>A village in the province of Zeeland, Netherlands.</note> my old friend and Brother **Pieter Pauwels**, who also for many years Christianly acquitted himself in the service of Elder in the church at **Norwich** <note>original: "Norwitz." Many Dutch Protestants fled to Norwich, England, to escape Spanish persecution.</note> during my time there: With him, I found a year and a day ago the draft of these two Treatises / and that for no other purpose / than to warn his children against this blind heap of **Anabaptist** <term>Herdoopscher: Literally "Re-baptizer." A derogatory term used by the state church for the various radical Reformation groups.</term> sects / in which he himself had been for some years in previous times through similar blindness. In this, he has Christianly followed the teaching and the command of God / notably in **Psalm 78** <note>This Psalm emphasizes teaching the next generation about the deeds of God and the errors of their ancestors.</note>. And although he (having never studied) has always supported himself with **farming** <note>original: "lantneeringe."</note> / nonetheless I found / that the Spirit of the Lord has been alive in him in this / and therefore he desired / to hand the same over to me entirely / to improve / to add or subtract / to put into good order / etc. to come to light under my name / just as he has entirely turned it over to me.

Secondly / let it not seem strange to you / that I here and there point to the **original text** <note>Referring to the original Greek and Hebrew of the Bible.</note> / also expressing some words more closely in our mother tongue according to the power of the same / the matter has required such / to point out the bold impudence of the Anabaptists / in using (or much more misusing) a passage of Holy Scripture here and there / also to provide a closer and clearer opening from the **original sources** <note>original: "originale fonteyne."</note> regarding the subject matter contested by these manifold sects.

Lastly, I wish to have this well-advised and prayed for / since even the Holy Scripture itself has its detractors / that this work of ours / coming into the hands of these sects from both sides / and he who can be made neither learned nor softened by it but much more takes his pleasure / in smearing this or that with the pen / that the same person does not (improperly) keep himself **nameless** / as a **certain someone** <note>original: "quidam," a Latin term for an unnamed person, often used dismissively in polemical writing.</note> has done for some time (in this his doing I can call him nothing else) / against the Dedicator **Joannes Beu** <note>Johannes Beeuwens, a Reformed minister in Middelburg.</note> / Minister of the Word of God in the church of Christ at **Middelburg** / alleging the texts of Holy Scripture / with such foundation and understanding / as (so they say) **Bartelt read the Psalter** <note>A Dutch idiom referring to someone who reads words without understanding their meaning or context.</note> / but if he knows a closer foundation / let him attack the matter itself / and from the foundation of the Holy Scripture (since here and there groundless foundations are drawn out) / let him act / read, and judge rightly.

<summary>In this preface, Herman Moded explains that the book's core was written by Pieter Pauwels, a former Anabaptist and elder in Norwich, to warn his children of sectarian errors. Moded also defends his use of original biblical languages and challenges anonymous critics to engage in honest scriptural debate.</summary>

<meta>This page is the author's preface to the reader. It follows the title page of Herman Moded’s 1603 work against Anabaptism. ### To the Christian Reader.

Attentive Reader, as I still find here and there some of the well-practiced <term>Brothers of the Cross: A term used for fellow believers who suffered persecution or "bore the cross" for their faith.</term>, whom I especially love, so a few years ago at West-Souburg I also found my old friend and brother Pieter Pauwels. For many years, during my time there, he served faithfully as an Elder in the church at Norwich <note>Norwich, England, was a major center for Dutch Protestant refugees fleeing Spanish persecution in the 16th century.</note> in a Christian manner. With him, I found a year or so ago the drafts of these two treatises. They were written for no other purpose than to warn his children against this blind heap of Anabaptist <term>Herdoopscher: Literally "Re-baptizing," the term Moded uses for the various Anabaptist groups.</term> sects, in which he himself had remained for some years in previous times through similar blindness. In this, he has Christianly followed the teaching and command of God, notably in Psalm 78. And although he (having never formally studied) always supported himself through farming <note>original: "lantneeringe," referring to earning a living from the land or rural trade.</note>, I nonetheless found that the Spirit of the Lord was living within him in this work. Therefore, he desired to hand the whole matter over to me to improve, to add or subtract as needed, and to put into good order, etc., so that it might come to light under my name, just as he surrendered it entirely to me.

Secondly, do not let it seem strange to you that I here and there point to the original text <note>Moded is referring to the original Greek and Hebrew of the Bible.</note>, and also express some words more closely in our mother tongue based on the strength of the same. The matter required this in order to point out the bold shamelessness of the Anabaptists in their use (or much rather, their misuse) here and there of a passage of Holy Scripture. It was also done to provide a closer and clearer opening, from the original fountain <note>original: "fonteyne," a common metaphor for the original biblical languages.</note>, into the subject matter contested by these many various sects.

Lastly, I wish to have this well-warned and requested: since even the Holy Scripture itself has its detractors, this work of ours, coming into the hands of these two-sided sects, may result in them becoming neither more learned nor softened by it. Rather, their desire will be much more to stain this or that with their pens. Let such a person not (improperly) keep himself nameless, as a certain person <note>original: "quidam," a Latin term for "a certain someone" or "an anonymous individual."</note> did for a certain time (in this his doing I can call him nothing else) against the dedication of Joannes Hen. <note>Joannes Hendricx, a Reformed minister.</note>, Minister of the Word of God in the Church of Christ at Middelburg. He cited the texts of Holy Scripture with such a foundation and understanding as (as the saying goes) "Bartelt read the Psalter" <note>A Dutch proverb—"lezen als Bartelt de Psalter"—referring to someone who reads words without understanding their meaning or reads poorly.</note>. But if he seeks a closer foundation, let him attack the matter itself, and from the foundation of the Holy Scripture (rather than setting down here and there a proverb pulled up without foundation), read and judge rightly.

# To the Noble, Renowned, highly-learned, very wise and powerful Lords, my Lords the <term>States General: The sovereign governing body of the United Provinces of the Netherlands.</term> of the united Netherlands, **Herman Moded** wishes blessed Salvation and prosperity.

Noble and powerful Lords, just as it is the calling of an experienced <term>Physician: Literal: "Medicine-master" (Medecijn-meester).</term> to care for the physical man—not only by giving the patient good prescriptions, but also by warning him of everything that might hinder recovery or harm the patient—so it is also with a faithful minister of the Church of God. His duty toward the <term>flock of Christ</term> is not only to pasture them with upright and sound doctrine (which is food and medicine for the soul) but also to take care of them by faithfully pointing out how to remain protected from all unhealthy food that is harmful to the soul.

God’s goodness has indeed always placed this sound and necessary food in His church as spiritual nourishment for the comfort, health, and salvation of His elect. However, in the times of both the Old and the New Testament, this has never existed without trial, nor without opposition. From every side, it has had its attackers from many kinds of false sects and heretics (arisen from the sidelines). These opponents, like dogs with their <note>original: "suerdeech," meaning leaven or sourdough. This is a biblical metaphor (referencing Matthew 16:6) for corrupting influence or false teaching that spreads through the church.</note> leaven, [attack] this sound doctrine, this upright and only true

<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication to the governing Lords States (the "Lords States" of the Dutch Republic) to the main body of the work. # Solid Foundation for the Introduction.

<margin>Ephesians 3:20</margin>
Christian Reader, it is a very lovely word, which rests on the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles. I believe in one **universal holy Church**, a **communion of saints** <note>This refers to the Apostles' Creed, a statement of faith used by most Christian denominations</note>; but it is more comforting to feel in the heart that one is incorporated into the same as a living member,
<margin>Ephesians 3:6</margin>
considering these benefits—as God's holy promises founded upon Jesus Christ our only **Savior** <note>original: "Salichmaker"</note>—likewise eternal welfare and salvation, belong only to the unique **body of Christ**, that is, his church:

# Nicolaes Storck, the first
### chief heretic, Father and founder of Anabaptism: combatant and opponent of the Holy Baptism of the children of the faithful.

Nicolaes Storck, the Father of Rebaptism <note>original: "Herdoop"; the practice of adult baptism, which the author views as a repetition of the sacrament</note>, born in Cygnea <note>The Latin name for the city of Zwickau</note> in Zwickau, rose up in the year fifteen hundred and twenty-one. # Ioannes Denck, the fifth sect of the Rebaptizers.

<margin>Here one rebaptizer fights against the other.</margin>
In the year 1526, the fifth sect of the rebaptizers <note>The term "Herdoopers" or "Wederdoopers" refers to the Anabaptists, who believed that infant baptism was invalid and that believers should be baptized again as adults.</note> emerged, the foundation of which was laid by Ioannes Denck, a schoolmaster in Nuremberg; a learned and experienced man in the Latin language, who agrees well with the other rebaptizers in opposing infant baptism. But on the point of the Civil Authority <note>original: "Ouerheydt" — This refers to the role of the state and magistrates, whom many Anabaptists refused to recognize or serve.</note>, he is strongly opposed and an enemy to the common rebaptizers. He also holds that one may take a proper oath, and swear faithfully, if love and discretion require it. He holds children free from original sin, which he believes can make no one—whether young or an adult who has come to understanding—damned; thus reviving the old heresy of Pelagius <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) was a theologian who taught that humans could take the first steps toward salvation by their own efforts, effectively denying the necessity of divine grace and the doctrine of original sin.</note>, from the year 399. # Melchior Rinck,

<margin>Rinck, being blinded himself, also blinds his disciples with divine inspiration.</margin>
For just as he, along with the other **Heretics**, has highly exalted and praised **Rebaptism** <note>Also known as Anabaptism; the practice of rebaptizing those who had already received infant baptism, which was a capital offense in many regions at the time.</note>, so too was he a powerful visionary and an experienced dreamer. He claimed everything happened through divine inspiration, praising and planting this so deeply into the hearts of his followers that they imagined themselves to be so "deified" <note>original: "vergodet"; a radical spiritualist concept where the believer felt they had become one with the divine nature, sometimes leading them to believe they were above moral laws.</note> that whatever they did had been revealed to them by the Father.

<margin>The devil is powerful in his works.</margin>
Thus it happened that one of his disciples, named Thomas Schucker, took his brother Leonard Schucker in the presence of both their father and mother during a full assembly of their preaching. He made him kneel down and called for a sword. When the father and some other disciples asked what he intended to do, he said: they should be of good cheer and remain quiet; nothing would happen except what God willed and what had been revealed to him. With this explanation, they were satisfied, firmly trusting in the will of God.

<margin>Just as Cain killed Abel, so Thomas here publicly murders his brother.</margin>
<margin>Is punished by the authorities.</margin>
Then Thomas struck off his brother’s head. Being imprisoned for this by the Authorities, he confessed until his death that it had been the will of God; and with such a confession, he remained steadfast until his execution. This gruesome example occurred in St. Gallen, Switzerland, in the year fifteen hundred and twenty-seven. See, Christian reader, what fruits these trees bear.

# Sebastian Franck, the ninth sect of the Anabaptists.

<margin>The sects of the Anabaptists number 44.</margin>
The ninth sect of the Anabaptists <note>original: "Herdoopers"; literally "Re-baptizers," a derogatory term used by critics of the movement.</note> was started by Sebastian Franck. Although he is an excellent chronicler <note>Sebastian Franck (1499–1542) was a famous German humanist and historian whose "Chronicle" was a massive, controversial work of the era.</note> and distinguishes the straying sects of the Anabaptists by dividing them into forty-four different beliefs, groups, and opinions—even saying that nearly every teacher has and advocates for his own particular opinion—Franck himself is not exempt from this. Indeed, he may rightly be named the forty-fifth opinion, and is placed here in the order as the ninth. This Franck, although he keeps himself quiet regarding the matter of rebaptism, nevertheless his disciples hold nothing of infant baptism.

<margin>Franck’s [work is] a labyrinth and full of slander.</margin>
He also desires to have an invisible church <note>The "Invisible Church" was a radical spiritualist concept; Franck believed the true church was a spiritual community of the heart, not an organized institution with buildings or officials.</note>; he considers all sermons, sacraments, and ceremonies to be nothing but a puppet show. Indeed, he believes there are no ceremonies on earth that can stain a good conscience. Therefore, he believes no one should put themselves in mortal danger for the sake of "dead things." Instead, out of love, one may be fully and physically present with everyone—even at the Pope’s Mass and other idolatry—as long as the spirit does not consent to it. Consequently, he regards all martyrs who refused to touch such idolatry and preferred to suffer the pain of martyrdom as "dried-up traitors" <note>original: "utgedroochde verraserije"; Franck was highly critical of traditional martyrdom, viewing it as a stubborn attachment to outward forms rather than inward spiritual freedom.</note> to themselves.

<margin>Franck, a public slanderer of God’s holy word.</margin>

# Melchior Rinck,

<margin>Rinck, being blinded, also blinds his disciples with divine inspiration.</margin>

# Sebastian Franck, the ninth sect of the Anabaptists.

<margin>There are 44 sects of Anabaptists.</margin>
The ninth sect of the Re-baptizers <note>original: "Herdoopers"; a term used by critics to emphasize that Anabaptists were "rebaptizing" those already baptized as infants.</note> was started by Sebastian Franck. Even though this Franck keeps quiet regarding the act of re-baptism itself, his disciples nonetheless hold no regard for infant baptism.

Therefore, he believes no one should put themselves in mortal danger for "dead things" <note>By "dead things," Franck referred to outward rituals like the Mass or physical baptism, which he believed had no spiritual value compared to the inner spirit.</note>. # Melchior Hofman, the tenth Arch-heretic and Father of the Dutch Anabaptists.

<margin>Melchior Hofman brings, as the first, re-baptism into the Netherlands.</margin>

This Melchior Hofman established the tenth sect of the Anabaptists <note>original: "Herdoopers," literally "Re-baptizers."</note>. For since in Germany nearly every teacher pursued his own particular heresy and sect, and each instructed and taught his followers according to his own opinion, so also has this Hofman come from Strasbourg <note>original: "Straets-burch"</note> to Emden in East Friesland in the year 1528. There he taught and gathered a group <note>original: "Rot"; a derogatory term for a gang or rabble.</note> of about three hundred persons, both men and women, where he practiced and taught re-baptism very strictly as a requirement for the soul's salvation. And this Melchior was the first who brought and preached re-baptism in these Netherlands, so that he may rightly be called the Father of Re-baptism in the Netherlands.

# Obbo Philips

Obbo Philips <note>Obbo Philips (c. 1500–1568) was a foundational leader of the Dutch Anabaptists who eventually became disillusioned with the movement’s radicalism and withdrew.</note>, a learned man, was sent out to Leeuwarden by Bartholomeus Boecbinder, as was mentioned previously. This was the twelfth sect of the Anabaptists, which was called the Batenburg sect <note>The Batenburgers were the most radical, violent offshoot of the Anabaptists, led by Jan van Batenburg after the fall of Münster in 1535.</note>. They teach much about the mortification of the flesh, dying to the world, the "New Creature," and so on.

From this sect another emerged, after their commissioners, Anthonis Kistemaker and Jacob Cramer, had returned home. They had brought back a report concerning the prosperity of Münster, and a large company had gathered to hear the new tidings at the house of Eppe Pieters, on the Sand <note>Refers to "Het Zand," an area in or near Leeuwarden.</note>. Among them was one Herman Pieters, a shoemaker, also known as "Father on the Sand." He laid himself upon a bed, half-full and drunk, and presented himself as the true Messiah <note>original: "Messiam"</note> who would deliver them all. Shouting dreadfully and horribly while lying in bed like a drunken swine: "Strike dead! Strike dead! Monks, priests, and all authorities over the whole world! Your deliverance is at hand! # Recantation of Obbo Philips.

<margin>Obbo earnestly admonishes his brother Dirk Philips and Menno to desist, but in vain.</margin>
Obbo made it known to the brothers, Menno <note>Menno Simons (1496–1561), the former priest whose name became the namesake for the Mennonites.</note> and Dirk <note>Dirk Philips (1504–1568), Obbo’s brother and a major theologian of the early peaceful Anabaptist movement.</note>, earnestly admonishing them, and acknowledged my <term>commissioning<note>original: "sendinge," referring to the formal act of being sent out as an apostle or minister.</note></term> as wrongful, and that I was deceived in that same matter; and I wished from my heart that they had not accepted such an office. I wished to free my soul by this confession before them, acknowledging my guilt in the deception; they may then do what they will, and may yet do. I thank the kind, gracious, and merciful God, who has opened my eyes, humbled my soul, changed my heart, looked upon my spirit and understanding with favor, and gave me a confession of my sins; and when I still think of the <term>deception<note>original: "verleydinge," often implying being led astray or seduced by false teachings.</note></term> that occurred among the brothers in Amsterdam, at Oldeklooster <note>A Cistercian monastery near Bolsward seized by radical Anabaptists in 1535; the ensuing siege resulted in hundreds of deaths.</note>, at Hazerswoude <note>original: "Assersau."</note>, at the Dam, on the Sand <note>Referring to the 1535 "naked runners" incident and the attempted coup in Amsterdam by radical Anabaptist factions.</note>, and above all at Münster <note>The Münster Rebellion (1534–1535), where radical Anabaptists established a "New Jerusalem" characterized by polygamy and violence, which ended in a brutal massacre.</note>, my soul grieves and is terrified thereat; I remain silent regarding all those false commissionings, prophecies, visions, dreams, revelations, and unspeakable <term>spiritual pride<note>original: "geestelicke hooverdie."</note></term>, which immediately from the start broke in among the brothers; for he who was baptized today, cried out tomorrow against all the godless, that they must be rooted out. # Recantation of Obbo Philips.

<center>David <note>This likely refers to David Joris, a prominent and controversial Anabaptist leader, or the "Promised David" figure popular in radical millenarian circles.</note></center>

...the kingdom of Christ here on earth for a thousand years <note>Refers to millenarianism, the belief in a literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth, which was central to the radical Anabaptists in Münster.</note>, the incarnation <note>original: "mensch wordinge," referring to the theological debate over how Christ took on human flesh.</note>, Baptism, Faith, the Lord’s Supper, double marriage <note>original: "dubbelde echte," a controversial practice among some radicals involving "spiritual" or polygamous unions.</note>, free will, predestination, willful sin unto death, the promised David, etc. And they will damn them all with bans <note>The "Ban" was the practice of excommunication and social shunning used strictly by Anabaptist groups.</note>, slanders, scolding, character assassination, judging them as heretics, the godless, and so on.

The Anabaptists are full of slanders and character assassination.

One says this, another says that, so that a sensible person may well say with truth that it is no church of God, but a cave of the devil, and a desolate abomination full of hate, envy, feigning, hypocrisy, contempt, scorn, and wrath. <margin>
The Anabaptists are a cave of the devil, a desolate abomination.
</margin>

And just as that beginning, the <term>commissioning<note>original: "sendinghe," the formal act of being sent by God or the church to preach.</note></term>, and the Apostolic office—along with [the roles of] Elijah, Enoch <note>Prophetic figures from the Bible whom radical leaders often claimed to personify.</note>, and all the Teachers—began, so too has the end revealed itself and been sufficiently shown. Anyone who does not wish to be completely blind can easily notice how one fails here and another there; one causes offense here, and another an uprising there.

<margin>
The Anabaptists cause nothing but offense and uprising.
</margin>

And if I were to say everything in full that is known to me—concerning the commissioning, the office, the teaching, and the teachers, all of whom I have known and what each stood upon—it would be far too much; indeed, it would be quite sorrowful to hear and also not profitable to reveal. These, thus far, are the own words of the recantation of Obbo Philips, copied from his book titled: *The Confession of Obbo Philips*.

# Adam Pastor, the fifteenth Arch-heretic of the Anabaptist Sect.

<margin>Disunity of the rebaptizers.</margin>

# Menno Simons.

...a child, as before, would say: "by no means."

<margin>Psalm 24:4</margin>
So then, simply to point out the contents of this Psalm without further explanation, you find herein two instructive parts that set before us the Kingdom of Christ here on earth. The first is how the subjects of this kingdom shall conduct themselves here, up until the 7th verse. The second part is the glorious entry of Christ into His kingdom, where the godly—God’s children—are exhorted as to how they shall receive this, their King Christ. 

Contained within the first part—concerning how the subjects of Christ, as His people, shall conduct themselves here in His Church—is also this: not to swear falsely. Take note of these words: here is no prohibition against swearing, but against swearing falsely. Swearing, then, is not only permitted in the Kingdom of Christ (that is, His Church), but is moreover explicitly commanded, as we shall hear hereafter. 

Therefore, those in authority are punishable in God's eyes who are either negligent toward their subjects in this matter or who look through their fingers <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to intentionally overlook or ignore a transgression.</note> at it. For in the kingdom of Christ there are always shortcomings, and it also has need of this teaching and exhortation to bring to memory the everlasting commandment of God: *Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor*. That is to say: your Oath, when necessity or love for your neighbor requires it, shall be without falsehood, upright, and true. 

Has this not been quite neatly volleyed <note>original: "af ghekaetst," a metaphor from ball games (like tennis or handball) meaning to skillfully hit a ball back, or in this context, to successfully refute an argument.</note> back at Menno?

<meta>This page continues the author's polemic against Menno Simons, the Anabaptist leader. Menno Simons, throwing a dirty rag <note>original: "vuyle lappe"; a 16th-century idiom for a worthless or contemptible addition to an argument.</note> into the mix—though he is not esteemed by the world—does that not fit well here, Reader? Likewise, [he claims] these words are full of spirit and wisdom, etc.

Now, concerning what Menno says with these words—that in the New Testament one must use "yes" and "no" [instead of an oath]—I answer: To use the words "yes" and "no" in place of the **Oath** (intending to banish it from the New Testament) is (as shall be explained) directly contrary to God’s command, God’s will, and His honor. It is also against necessity, utility, and love for one's neighbor. Furthermore, it is against a well-ordered **civil society** <term>policie: from the Greek 'politeia', referring to the organized government and legal order of a state.</term> and the proper respect due to God’s servants, the **Authorities**. 

For if we were required to be satisfied with a simple "yes" and "no" in these matters—given that all men are subject to vanity and are liars—then not only would God’s honor and will be diminished, but a total confusion and barbaric behavior would break into our civil life and trade. 

<margin>
Psalm 116:11 <note>The verse states: "I said in my haste, All men are liars."</note>
Romans 3:4 <note>The verse states: "Let God be true, but every man a liar."</note>
Psalm 29:6
</margin>

Firstly, then, regarding God’s command and will: who would be so barbaric and shameless as to say or believe that God is changeable in His eternal command and will? Therefore, God’s holy commandment concerning the oath remains firm, immovable, and forever lasting. Because of this, the <term>Authorities</term> <note>original: *Overheyt*. # Menno Simons

...[his own commandments] <note>The sentence continues from the previous page, referring to Christ's relationship to the Law.</note> here he does not wish to improve, nor even—as if they were reinforced by an eternally lasting decree—to take them away. Rather, he wishes much more to explain them soundly and to remove what has been added to them as a corruption; for 

<margin>Matthew 5:17, 18</margin>
Christ says in that same chapter, indeed in express words, that he did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. He adds to this his customary oath: **"I say to you truly: until heaven and earth pass away, not the smallest letter of the law shall pass away, etc."** Likewise, 

<margin>Matthew 5:33</margin>
just before this (showing that this is far from Christ’s meaning), he says very clearly that one must not break an oath, nor swear falsely. Tell me now: are these words, "but I say to you **Swear not at all**," meant to explain the <term>Oath</term> <note>The author views the oath as a sacred testimony of truth used in legal and spiritual contexts, whereas the Mennonites viewed it as strictly forbidden by the New Testament.</note>, or to abolish it? If they were meant to abolish it, what then remains of God's everlasting commandment: **"You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor."** Likewise: **"You shall not** 

<margin>Leviticus 19:12</margin>
**swear falsely by my name, and profane the name of your God."** If the name of God is profaned by false swearing, then it follows that it is sanctified by truthful swearing. Now, his name is profaned by adding to it, taking away from it, or substituting something else in its place, or even by using it lightly—which is undoubtedly no small profanation of the name of God. Furthermore, this everlasting commandment of God is not <term>ceremonial</term> <note>In Reformation theology, "ceremonial" laws were Jewish rituals abolished by Christ (like animal sacrifice), while "moral" laws were considered eternally binding.</note>, but has its own glorious purpose.

<summary>The author argues that Christ’s prohibition of swearing in Matthew 5 was intended to correct corruptions and forbid lighthearted or false swearing, rather than to abolish the moral law regarding truthful oaths.</summary>

The word **"at all"** <note>Referring to the phrase "Swear not at all" from Matthew 5:34.</note>, which is pushed with great misunderstanding, you cannot by virtue of the text apply to the substance of the Oath; rather, it must necessarily be joined to the form and the types of abuse, as if Christ meant to say: "You shall swear neither directly nor indirectly with these or similar added types." <margin>Notice the mad insanity of the rebaptizers.</margin>

# Of the Flemish

<margin>Driven out.</margin>
...[ca]st out <note>original: "sten", likely the suffix of a verb like *verstooten* meaning cast out</note> in the person of the son of Jan vande Walle, at West-Souburg. Notwithstanding the fact that he is sometimes not in his right mind or understanding, he is forced to obtain his food, drink, and whatever else he needs from outside the natural household <term>hupse|an archaic term for home or farmstead</term>. He is not permitted to speak to his own mother or brothers, who belong to this sect. They even have his linen washed by others, and the only "mercy" he receives is that he is allowed to lodge in a dog kennel standing in the courtyard.

<margin>Judgment of the Anabaptists.</margin>
They strongly maintain and assert that the godless, upon dying, do not suffer the pains of hell or the fires of hell until Christ, coming for judgment, shall reunite the body with the soul once more.

<margin>Anabaptist dissension.</margin>
Regarding the humanity of Christ, they are also in disagreement. For just as we have presented the opinion of Menno [Simons] above—noting that Menno is in conflict with himself—likewise they conflict with one another in their *Sacrifice* or *Martyr’s Book* <note>original: *Offer ofte Martelaer boec*, referring to the famous Anabaptist collection *Het Offer des Heeren*</note>, as they call it. Even in their final hour, as they went to their deaths, they disagreed, as can be read concerning Joos Kint in his confession on page 112, and Maeyken Boosers on page 220. There, they died maintaining the belief that Christ is not the Son of David <note>A reference to the "Celestial Flesh" doctrine, which held that Jesus did not take his human nature from Mary but brought it from heaven.</note>. On the other hand, in the same *Sacrifice Book* on page 21, it is written of Jan Claessen, and of Joos Verbeke in the *Songs* (page 21), that both cried out at their deaths: "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me," etc. Here, these last two are set against the first two, and that in their hour of greatest need. How shameful and contradictory!

<margin>Lubbert pronounces judgment upon himself.</margin>

# Robert Robertssen.

Robert Robertssen, the **Miracle** man, living in the city of Amsterdam; by profession or trade, a schoolmaster and a maker of sea charts <note>Maps used for maritime navigation.</note>. He was called the "Miracle Man" by Pieter D. B., the leader of the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wederdoopers"; literally "Re-baptizers," a radical Reformation movement.</note>, in his "answer-song." This man [Robertssen] was associated with Lubbert Geertsen, whose "beast of burden" or "carrying little donkey" he describes himself as being. He was especially Lubbert's personal secretary, as the one who was entrusted to bring Lubbert's own books or writings to the press, as was previously stated. He was (I say), along with his master Lubbert, a special instrument in the building up of these aforementioned new Frisian sects. However, he was rewarded by his "good friend"—despite the faithful service he rendered to him and his company—in the same way they reward almost all their people: with the cut of the ban <note>Excommunication; being formally cut off from the religious community.</note>, and he was handed over to the devil at the end of the year 1591.

<margin>A new Anabaptist dispute.</margin>
The cause is this: Robert had written a small book, two quires in size <note>A "quire" is a set of sheets folded into each other; two quires suggests a pamphlet of approximately 16 to 24 pages.</note>, which Lubbert, along with some other teachers, read through. It did not please them, and they pointed out two or three errors to him. To this, Robert answered that it was true; he well acknowledged the errors as far as the spelling and arrangement were concerned, but in the sense and right understanding, he said his little book was correct. He was also willing to withhold the books (of which 500 had been printed) from distribution, were it not that he had already incurred too great an expense for them...

Note well, dear reader, what spirit this is; just like one of the first and most highly famous of all, it is masterfully driven by that same spirit of error <note>The author is accusing Robertssen of being possessed by the same "delusion" as other famous heretics</note>.

There have recently arisen three more sects of the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>original: "Dooperen". A radical Reformation movement that practiced adult baptism and often lived in separated communities</note> out of the "Flemish House" <note>A major branch of the Anabaptist movement in the Netherlands</note>, who are named the <term>House-buyers</term> <note>original: "hupscoopers". A faction named after a dispute over the purchase of a meeting house</note>, the Counter-House-buyers, and the Neutralists. These sects ban and excommunicate one another by the hundreds at a time. One side acknowledges the purchase of a certain house—bought by Thomas Beenkens, Bishop at Franeker—to have been done well and without deceit. The leaders of this house-purchase alongside Thomas Beenkens are, in particular, Jacob Pieters vander Meulen (Bishop at Haarlem and the champion of <term>Marital Avoidance</term> <note>original: "Echtmijdinghe". The controversial practice of requiring a member to shun their own spouse if that spouse was excommunicated</note>), Hans de Wever, Philips Warnaerts, and Lambert Janssen. Against these are many others of their teachers who strongly maintain that the purchase of the aforementioned house was done deceitfully and fraudulently, and is therefore worthy of excommunication.

### Messenger of Truth.

Namely this: that the healthy early <note>original: "primitive"</note> church applied all its industry and diligence—likewise holding its Synods <term>Synods</term> <note>Formal assemblies of church leaders gathered to discuss and decide on points of doctrine or administration</note> in times of need—to harmoniously suppress, based on the foundation of the Holy Scripture, all foreign teachings and sects that had broken in, whether from the side or even from within the church. This was done to preserve the health of the body of Christ <note>A common biblical metaphor where the community of believers is compared to a physical body with Christ as the head</note> well everywhere, also by following the Apostolic rule simply and directly <note>original: "slecht en recht"</note> within the same, without veering from it to the right hand or to the left. 

For a little leaven <note>original: "suerdeechs"; a biblical reference to how a small amount of yeast affects the entire batch of dough, used here to describe how small errors can corrupt the whole church</note> (however small it may be) leavens the whole dough over time. The "shadow" is that these subsequent times (as is evident here) have looked little at this mark and have not strived for it. Instead, men have been busy with the shadow, using human wisdom to create new rules, decrees, and statutes—yet under the title of being useful for the utility and well-being of the churches. In reality, these tend toward nothing but dominion and the pleasing of men, regarding Christ’s institution, the Apostles’ teaching, and the purity of the Apostolic church with little respect, in order to master them and shape them according to their own wisdom—

It is also clear from this that they certainly remain silent about Christ being the Son of Man, both of which sonships <note>Refers to Christ being both the "Son of God" and the "Son of Man."</note> must be equally precious to us. ### 1. Dialogue
<meta>catchword: discourse</meta>

...origin of the flesh of Christ to be from heaven, but the essence of the flesh itself from **Mary**. This man also wants to have his say, and like **Judas**, leave a name behind; he has likewise learned his <term>dialectics: the art of logical argument</term> in the school of "a fool in repose" <note>original Latin: *stultum in supino*. This is a grammatical pun playing on the Latin "supine" (a verbal noun) to suggest someone who is both intellectually lazy and foolish</note>.

The ninth, Kaus Bisschop, in the *Frankenthal Protocol* <note>The Frankenthal Disputation was a famous 1571 debate where the Elector Palatine attempted to reconcile Anabaptists with the state church</note>, folio 136, says that one should conclude as if we held that Christ had not been conceived of the **Virgin Mary**; we do not say that, we wish to leave it to God. ...friend; I stand before the man, and not behind him." <note>This refers to the Anabaptists’ use of literalisms and semantic riddles to avoid direct answers or oaths.</note> Also: "I shall not go into the city or village and scatter with a wagon, or travel with a ship therein." Also: "I cannot do it on that foot, but will do it immediately on the other foot." <note>These phrases illustrate what the author considers deceptive wordplay or "tricks" (rancken) used to evade clarity.</note> Such tricks they have much in common with hypocrites and the feigned, of whom Peter <margin>2 Peter 2:1, 2, 3</margin> writes, as those who take pleasure in their own deceptions, etc.

In their croaking, groaning, and sighing, and in their silent prayers—to which no one coming into their assembly can say "Amen" <margin>1 Corinthians 14:16, 17</margin>—they act against the teaching of Paul.

What do you think of this, my Brother? Are your eyes not yet fully opened? Do you think that these people are still building upon the foundation of Jesus Christ? And does it still offend you when they are placed on the same level as the ancient heretics and the Pope? Do you still think it a hard saying when it is said of all these people generally that they have no part or portion with the children of God, so long as they remain in such error?

->The Simple Man<-

Oh no, my dear brother; I thank the good God who has sent me to you, by whose instruction my eyes have been opened, so that I now clearly—as if by the bright sun—see and acknowledge the wandering paths that I have walked for a long time in ignorance. I lament this before the Lord: that I did not look back or ask for counsel sooner. It would seem to me...

<summary>The author concludes a list of Anabaptist linguistic deceptions and criticizes their silent or unintelligible prayers. The "Simple Man" character finally concedes that he has been misled and expresses gratitude for being shown the "true" path.</summary>
<keywords>Anabaptists, deception, silent prayer, Paul, Peter, conversion, heresy, semantic tricks, simple man</keywords>

# 1. Dialogue #

[...know] <note>This completes the word "know" from the previous page's catchword.</note> that these heretics stand upon the foundation of Christ? I have heard too much testimony of the truth concerning that, and you have (for which I thank you greatly) revealed their basis to me so plainly, that I know no better than to count these groups the same as the heretic Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings on the nature of the Godhead were condemned as heresy at the Council of Nicaea.</note>. Indeed, I doubt whether they do not stand in a more impure state in some things than the Papists <note>A term used by reformers to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> themselves; though I assume there is not much to choose between them, so that I can no longer be offended, nor is it a hard saying for me to hear further. For I have heard so much that I am convinced in my heart by the truth that I have labored in vain for so long and missed the right path. And as I have been led astray until now, I will, with God's help, go and warn all simple people of the wrong ways and deceitful seductions of the aforementioned sects and these divided Anabaptists <note>original: "wederdoopers." Your pure intent and purpose are good, but how will you go about it? They are very cunning and will seek to trap you in your own words; if you then have no good proof, they will break out into slandering.

->The Simple Man<-

I shall in all things refer to the instruction of truth, which I have now fully heard—at least as much as shall be necessary for my defense.

# Dialogue.

...cunning wandering paths <note>The Dutch fragment "lep" likely completes the word "geslepen," meaning cunning, devious, or slippery. The sentence begins mid-thought.</note> / from which I have been brought free, which were previously shown to me by all these **sectarian spirits**; of which I am now certainly informed by the truth, as I have also visibly seen the great misunderstanding of all these teachers, the **wandering spirits**, to whom we previously entrusted ourselves. The practice of rebaptizing adults, which gave the "Anabaptist" movement its name.</note>, the **Ban**, and other customs. 

But I am even more informed regarding **Infant Baptism**, of which I now fully understand Christ to be the Author; it was used by the Apostles, confirmed by the Church Fathers, and thus has remained in use until now without any opposition, until these fellows, the **rebaptizers**, rose up in our times. They have highly praised **rebaptism** to us, and yet it is nothing other than a cursed beginning from **Nicolas Storch** <note>Nicolas Storch (d. 1525) was one of the "Zwickau Prophets." Also, it is a collection of lying fictions to say that infant baptism was supposedly instituted by **Hyginus** <note>original: "Igenio". Referring to Pope Hyginus (2nd century), whom radicals often blamed for "corrupting" the church with non-biblical traditions.</note> or **Innocent**, or **Pope Nicholas**, or even by the false apostles.

Furthermore, I am now instructed by the testimony of the Fathers and the confession of the **Martyrs**, following from the times of the Apostles down to our own times, who were all of one mind in the faith, of one...

# Dialogue

...and also such as the Lord shall give me to speak through his Holy Spirit. What do you think, my brother, will that be well?

->Instruction of Truth<- <note>original: "Bericht der waerheyt," an allegorical figure representing orthodox teaching.</note>

May the Lord give you grace and wisdom for that; and if you have need of me, I do not wish to be spared—speak to me. You know where I may be found, and if anything else comes to your mind, you may reveal it to me; I wish to be helpful to you in all things where I can promote the glory of God and the benefit of the simple person.

->Simple Person<- <note>original: "Eenvoudich Mensche," representing the common layperson seeking religious clarity.</note>

I thank you heartily, my good friend and dear brother, for the good instruction that you have given me, and for satisfying me in all things with the truth. I hope that our dialogue shall not be fruitless, and it seems good to me that we leave it at this for the present time. May the Lord make us understanding and guide us with his Holy Spirit, to remain steadfast and fervent in the upright faith and Christian walk according to his pleasure.

->Instruction of Truth<-

Amen, may the eternal and merciful God grant us that, so that we may gather together on the sure, enduring foundation <note>original: "fundamēt"</note> declared by the Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, into the single sheepfold <note>original: "schaepskope" (likely a variant of "schaapskooi"), a common biblical metaphor for the Church.</note> of the faithful shepherd Jesus Christ <note>original: "Christi Jesu"</note>, who grants us grace for that through the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, Amen, Amen.
